city.name: Yorktown
summary: Yorktown was a small tobacco port on a bluff over the York River, a few dozen houses, stores and warehouses along one main street. In August 1781 Lord Cornwallis brought his army of about 8,000 here to make a base for the Royal Navy, and fortified the town and Gloucester Point across the river.

Washington and Rochambeau marched south from New York, while the Comte de Grasse's French fleet beat off the Royal Navy and closed Chesapeake Bay. From 28 September some 17,000 French and American troops besieged the town, dug their trenches closer, stormed two redoubts and battered the defences. Cornwallis surrendered on 19 October 1781, and major fighting in the war was over.
city.note: River and shoreline from today's OpenStreetMap; the 1781 shore was much the same. Streets follow the 1691 town plan, which today's streets keep. The British inner line, the second parallel and surviving buildings follow OpenStreetMap's mapping of Colonial National Historical Park. The first parallel, the camps and the scuttled ships are placed after period siege maps and are approximate. Houses between the streets are generated.

properties.name: Road to Hampton
description: The road south out of Yorktown. On 19 October 1781 the British garrison marched down it, between a line of French troops on one side and Americans on the other, to lay down their arms.

properties.name: Yorktown
description: About 60 or 70 houses, stores and taverns along Main Street, with warehouses on the beach below the bluff. In the 1750s it was Virginia's busiest tobacco port, but trade had fallen away by 1781.
Allied guns pounded the town from 9 October. Many houses were wrecked, and townspeople who stayed sheltered in caves dug into the bluff.

properties.name: Nelson House
description: The brick house of Thomas Nelson Jr., a signer of the Declaration of Independence and in 1781 governor of Virginia, who commanded the Virginia militia in the siege.
The story goes that Nelson told the Allied gunners to fire on his own house, since British officers were using it. Cannonballs are still lodged in its east wall.

properties.name: Custom House
description: A brick store built about 1721 by the merchant Richard Ambler, collector of customs for the port of York. Tobacco bound for Britain was cleared here.

properties.name: Swan Tavern
description: The town's main tavern from 1722, facing the courthouse across Main Street. What stands today is a rebuilding of the 1930s.

properties.name: Dudley Digges House
description: A frame house of about 1760, home of Dudley Digges, a member of Virginia's revolutionary Committee of Safety.

properties.name: Grace Church
description: Built in 1697 of marl, a soft stone of fossil shells cut from the river bluff. The British used it as a magazine during the siege. It was burned in 1814 and again in 1863, but its marl walls still stand.

properties.name: Moore House
description: Augustine Moore's farmhouse a mile east of town. On 18 October 1781 officers of both sides met here and drew up the terms of surrender, signed by Cornwallis the next morning.

properties.name: British inner line
description: Cornwallis's main defence: a ring of earthworks, redoubts and batteries round the landward side of the town, from the river above it to the river below. About 7,500 British and German troops held it.
Short of tools and men, the British were still digging when the Allies arrived. On 29 September Cornwallis pulled his troops back from the outer works into this line, hoping for relief by sea.

properties.name: Hornwork
description: A large work across the Hampton road, the strongest point of the British line. The Allied second parallel was dug within 300 yards of it.

properties.name: Fusiliers' Redoubt
description: A detached British redoubt by the river west of town, held by the Royal Welch Fusiliers. The French attacked it on 30 September and were driven off; it held to the end.

properties.name: Pigeon Quarter redoubts
description: British outer redoubts on the plateau south-west of town. Cornwallis abandoned them on the night of 29 September, and the Allies took them over the next day as part of their own lines.

properties.name: Redoubt 9
description: One of two British redoubts in front of the main line, near the river east of town. They stopped the Allies from carrying their second parallel to the water.
On the night of 14 October, 400 French grenadiers and chasseurs under the Comte de Deux-Ponts stormed it with the bayonet, losing about 100 men.

properties.name: Redoubt 10
description: A small square redoubt on the bluff above the river. At the same hour as the French attack on Redoubt 9, about 400 Americans under Lieutenant Colonel Alexander Hamilton rushed it with unloaded muskets and took it in under ten minutes.
With both redoubts taken, the Allies extended their second parallel to the river, and the British position became hopeless.

properties.name: Gloucester Point works
description: Across the river, about 700 British troops under Lieutenant Colonel Banastre Tarleton and Lieutenant Colonel Thomas Dundas held a line of entrenchments and redoubts across the point. French cavalry and Virginia militia hemmed them in after a skirmish on 3 October.
On the night of 16 October Cornwallis tried to ferry his army across to Gloucester and break out north. A storm scattered the boats and the attempt failed.

properties.name: Allied first parallel
description: On the night of 6 October, 1,500 men with picks and shovels dug a trench about 2,000 yards long, some 600 to 800 yards from the British line, while a storm hid the noise. The French held the left, the Americans the right, down to the river below the town.
Batteries were built along it, and on 9 October Washington himself fired the first American gun.

properties.name: French trench above the town
description: A separate French trench and battery west of Yorktown Creek, facing the Fusiliers' Redoubt. Its guns also fired on British ships in the river.

properties.name: Allied second parallel
description: Begun on the night of 11 October, about 300 to 400 yards from the British works, close enough for the guns to batter the town at short range. Redoubts 9 and 10 blocked its eastern end.

properties.name: French Grand Battery
description: The largest French battery on the first parallel. Its heavy guns and mortars opened fire on 9 October and soon silenced most of the British guns facing it.

properties.name: American Grand Battery
description: The main American battery near the river end of the first parallel. Washington fired its first gun on the afternoon of 9 October.

properties.name: French camp
description: About 7,800 French soldiers under the Comte de Rochambeau camped here on the Allied left, west of Yorktown. Most had sailed from France in 1780; another 3,000 under the Marquis de Saint-Simon came with de Grasse's fleet.

properties.name: American camp
description: About 8,800 Americans, Continentals and Virginia militia, camped in woods on the Allied right. Many had marched 450 miles from New York in August and September.

properties.name: Washington's headquarters
description: George Washington pitched his tents between the American and French camps, close to Rochambeau's headquarters, so the two generals could meet daily.

properties.name: Scuttled British ships
description: Cornwallis had some 60 vessels at Yorktown. To keep a French landing off the beach he sank about a dozen transports and small ships in a line along the shore, leaving their masts showing.
On 10 October French hot shot set fire to the 44-gun HMS Charon, which burned and sank off the town with several transports.

properties.name: HMS Charon
description: A 44-gun British warship anchored between Yorktown and Gloucester. French guns set her on fire with heated shot on the night of 10 October and she burned to the waterline.

properties.name: Surrender Field
description: At 2 pm on 19 October 1781 the British garrison, about 8,000 men, marched out between the Allied lines to this field and laid down their arms. Their bands are said to have played 'The World Turned Upside Down'.

Cornwallis stayed away, claiming illness. His deputy, Brigadier General Charles O'Hara, offered his sword to Rochambeau, who pointed him to Washington, who in turn sent him to his own deputy, Benjamin Lincoln. It was the last major battle of the war.
